Historical observations for this pairing come from thousands of weather stations throughout the United States, some of which have been in place for a century or more. Data have been adjusted to account for any biases that might be introduced by factors such as station moves or changes in measuring instruments.

Model outputs are based on a set of 16 global climate models that reflect scientists’ current understanding of how greenhouse gases warm the atmosphere; how this heat moves between the atmosphere, water, and land; and the resulting effects on weather patterns and precipitation. These same 16 models were used in the most recent National Climate Assessment. The modeled lines are smoother than the historical trends because the project team averaged 16 models together and also applied an 11-year smoothing filter, both of which smooth out year-to-year variability. However, the shaded bands do include year-to-year variability.

For consistency, all precipitation is measured in inches of water—which means snowfall is converted to the liquid equivalent. The graph shows annual anomalies, or the difference from the average precipitation from 1901 to 2000.

As with all indicators calculated from climate model projections, there is uncertainty associated with the total annual precipitation indicator. Precipitation is more difficult to model than temperature, especially in regions with highly variable precipitation. There is some uncertainty regarding how precipitation patterns are projected to change under changing climate conditions, and while models might agree on the trend, they are not designed to predict which years are abnormally dry and which are abnormally wet. This leads to a wider spread between models for each year because they do not project the exact same interannual variations.
